summary: Moving to post-quantum cryptography often involves hybrid schemes that combine post-quantum and traditional asymmetric algorithms. This informational RFC defines terminology for such schemes, serving as a reference so documents and discussions about them use consistent words.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines shared terms for cryptographic schemes that combine post-quantum and traditional algorithms. The terms help other documents describe these combinations consistently.

questions: what is a pq/t hybrid scheme
what is a composite hybrid scheme
subtitle: Shared terminology for schemes that combine post-quantum and traditional algorithms.

tldr.problem: Documents use terms for post-quantum and traditional cryptographic combinations inconsistently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines shared terms for hybrid algorithms, cryptographic elements, protocols, properties, and certificates.
tldr.outcome: It is a terminology reference. It does not itself change or secure an Internet protocol.

today: RFC 9794 is an Informational RFC published in June 2025. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it is a terminology reference and reports no IANA actions.

sections.title: Why Hybrid Terminology Is Needed
sections.content:
The RFC explains that a sufficiently capable quantum computer could threaten some traditional public-key algorithms. A designer may combine a post-quantum algorithm with a traditional algorithm during a transition or to seek protection from different kinds of attackers.

The document uses PQ/T hybrid for combinations that include at least one post-quantum and one traditional algorithm. It provides a reference vocabulary rather than specifying a particular hybrid design.
sections.plainLanguage: A hybrid scheme uses both a post-quantum algorithm and a traditional algorithm. This RFC gives writers a shared name for that combination and its parts.

sections.title: Schemes and Cryptographic Elements
sections.content:
A multi-algorithm scheme combines algorithms with the same cryptographic purpose. In a PQ/T hybrid scheme, component algorithms work on the same input and their outputs are used together.

A composite scheme presents one interface of the same type as its component algorithms. A combiner is the method that combines those algorithms or their cryptographic elements. The RFC also defines PQ/PQ hybrid terminology for schemes whose components are all post-quantum.
sections.plainLanguage: A hybrid scheme combines algorithms that do the same kind of job. A composite scheme presents the combined result through one interface, while a combiner describes how the parts are joined.

sections.title: Composite and Non-Composite Protocols
sections.content:
A PQ/T hybrid protocol uses multiple algorithms with the same cryptographic function, including at least one post-quantum and one traditional algorithm. A protocol that offers a choice between the two but uses only one is not a hybrid protocol under this definition.

In a composite construction, cryptographic element formats change while protocol fields and message flow remain largely the same. In a non-composite construction, protocol fields or message flow change while component element formats remain the same. A protocol may use both approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: A composite design combines algorithm parts behind one cryptographic interface. A non-composite design keeps the parts separate and changes the protocol messages to use them.

sections.title: Properties of Hybrid Schemes
sections.content:
Hybrid confidentiality and hybrid authentication mean the relevant property holds while at least one component intended to provide it remains secure. Hybrid interoperability means two parties can complete an operation when they share support for at least one component algorithm.

The RFC explains that a scheme alone cannot always provide both interoperability and confidentiality. A protocol can address this with downgrade protection outside the cryptographic scheme. Backwards and forwards compatibility describe cases where parties can proceed using traditional or post-quantum components.
sections.plainLanguage: Different hybrid goals make different demands. For example, interoperability may allow a shared algorithm, while confidentiality may require using every component; a protocol needs safeguards when it supports both goals.

sections.title: Certificates and Security Scope
sections.content:
A PQ/T hybrid certificate contains public keys for at least one traditional and one post-quantum algorithm. A certificate with both keys does not by itself guarantee hybrid authentication of identity; the certificate chain and protocol determine that property.

This RFC defines security-related terms but says it has no security impact on Internet protocols. The security analysis for each hybrid scheme or protocol belongs in its own specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate can contain keys from both algorithm types, but the certificate alone does not prove that the whole identity check uses both. Each protocol must describe its own security properties.
